doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing with Kenny Davern
summary: Monk says Davern first gave him her name; she subbed with Greg Cohen on Davern's last gigs, praising his sound, space, and demanding encouragement.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Let me — I’m watching the time here — but I just wanted to toss a couple of names at you. We were taking about Kenny Davern earlier. And he’s the guy who first gave me your name.
Yep. Because we were taking about who to bring up to Hamilton.
You never caught me with Kenny.
We did a lot of gigs though, before he passed. You know I was subbing for I’m trying to name the bass player that he played with, Greg —

Greg Cohen. And so between me and Greg, we did most of Kenny’s gigs in the last couple of years. I loved playing with him. I liked the fact that he had a different approach to playing that music completely. In other words, he liked the openness, I loved the way James Chirillo played with him, because I felt like there was a lot of space. And I love space in music. And I don’t feel sometimes there is enough of it. It gets a little crowded there. And I never felt that way on Kenny’s gigs. I felt there was so much — Kenny never wasted notes. He just had one of the best sounds I’ve ever heard on clarinet. And he wanted you to play. He didn’t want you to take short solos. He encouraged you to play on solos sometimes. And I learned a lot. And sometimes it wasn’t feeling right and he’d turn around and say something you know what I mean? And he’d scare the hell out of you. But it was all out of encouragement. I just that that it really was on your side.
He wanted it to be good.

He wanted it to be really good. Really high standards. He really did. And often it was because he believed in you that he would say something in the first place. And I was pleased with that. This gets back to the women thing. I think sometimes guys are really scared to say something to a woman musician that they might say to a guy. And I’m like no, I’m one of the guys. I’m the one that has 22 years on the road. You can’t shock me. You know what I mean? I’ve always wanted to be treated like one of the guys. So tell me if I’m rushing or slowing down. Just tell me. I might get a little upset maybe back in the hotel room later, but I’m going to listen to you and I’m going to say okay, good. Maybe I wasn’t aware of that. Thank you. You know what I mean? Because how else do you grow © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
as a musician? I think of someone like Kenny as having the experience of playing with really great bass players and knows what he wants. Then tell me. Because I’m younger and maybe I just don’t know.
